title: Guru Arjan's martyrdom day
hook: in the June heat Sikhs hand out cold sweetened water to passers-by

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurpurab, the poet and commander. Your line was sword and song. Today, a harder day in the Sikh year, and a surprising way to keep it.

The night before, somebody's garage fills up with bags of ice. Big steel drums get rinsed out with a hose. There's a crate of milk, a sack of sugar, maybe a bottle of rose syrup, and a stack of paper cups as tall as a child. By mid-morning there's a table at a busy corner, it's well over a hundred degrees, and a line of teenagers stands in the traffic with trays, waving cars down. On day sixty-four, you were the driver being handed a cup. Today, step around to the other side of the table.
screen: `ICE AND STEEL DRUMS, THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `TRAYS HELD OUT INTO THE TRAFFIC.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: The stall is called a chhabeel. The word is usually traced to the Arabic sabil, a public water fountain given as charity, the kind built in Muslim cities from Cairo to Istanbul; a free drink of water is honored on more than one path. You already know whose day it is. On days sixty-three and sixty-four you met Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, held in Lahore in the summer of 1606, the first Sikh shaheed, and the line he held to: your will is sweet. Today isn't the story again; it's how the Sikh year keeps it. The anniversary falls in the hottest weeks, in May or June, depending on which calendar a gurdwara follows. Inside, there's kirtan of his hymns and an Ardas. Outside, the chhabeel. Here's how one actually runs. The drink is often kachi lassi: water with a little milk and sugar, sometimes rose syrup, poured over ice in those steel drums. It's handed out with both hands, to anyone, without asking a name or a faith: truck drivers, police officers, schoolkids, strangers. A good chhabeel ends up with more helpers than it planned, because people walking past stop to pour. Some run for an afternoon, some for a week. Notice who holds the trays: very often the young. That's how a memory four hundred years old gets handed on. Not as a lecture about cruelty, but as a job: standing in the heat, cooling someone else.
screen: `CHHABEEL — FROM SABIL, A FREE FOUNTAIN.` · `GURU ARJAN'S DAY, IN THE HEAT.` · `KACHI LASSI, ICE AND BOTH HANDS.` · `A MEMORY HANDED ON AS A JOB.` · then, large: `COOL WATER FOR ANYONE.`

segments.voice: If a glass of cool water is near, hold it, feel the cold in your hands, and take one slow sip; if not, just picture one. Think of someone worn out, overheated, overworked today, a delivery driver, a coworker, someone at home, and picture handing them the glass, and their face as they take it. If you pray, you can remember Guru Arjan's calm.
Chhabeel. A stall of cold sweetened drinks given free to passers-by, remembering Guru Arjan, who was martyred in the heat.
Your line: cool water for anyone. No name asked, no faith asked. Day one hundred fifty, done.

howItsDone: On and around the anniversary of Guru Arjan's martyrdom in June, Sikhs set up chhabeels, stalls handing out chilled sweetened drinks free to passers-by, alongside kirtan and prayers at the gurdwara.

notes: Ang 394 (tera kiya meetha lagai, Har Naam padarath Nanak mangai) paraphrased. Confirm Ang.
Details of the torture (hot plate, burning sand, the Ravi) given as 'Sikh tradition tells'. Confirm; handled soberly, without blaming any faith community.
Jahangir's memoir records his orders concerning the Guru; referenced in the trapdoor only. Confirm phrasing.
Chhabeel drink: often kachi lassi (water with milk and sugar) or sherbet. Confirm.

Reviewer edit: 'arrested in Lahore' changed to 'summoned to Lahore and taken into custody'. Who pressed for it (Jahangir's own motives, Chandu Shah, Prithi Chand's faction, court politics) is debated by historians; the script names only Jahangir's order, which his memoir records. Fork setup now says 'tradition says' for the torture details. Confirm.
Date: Nanakshahi June 16; by lunar reckoning it varies. The voice says 'in the hottest weeks ... on and around the anniversary'.
